source.title_on_document: Can large language models teach creativity? Cognitive gains, affective gaps, and distinct neural patterns

supplement.where: Appendix A: 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100288' (p. 12)
supplement.holds: Table S2 with pre- and post-test means and SDs for all three groups (the main text prints post-test means and SDs only for the AI group), Fig. S1 and Table S1 (fNIRS probe layout), Fig. S2 (learning intention), the human instructors' scripts, the backup learning materials, and the subjective questionnaire items.

paper_design_summary: 95 university-recruited adults in Shanghai were randomly assigned to 8-10 minutes of one-to-one creativity instruction from ChatGPT-4.0 (n = 31), one-to-one instruction from a trained human instructor following a script (n = 34), or a control condition of quiet rest (n = 30). All took an Alternative Uses Task before instruction (books) and after instruction (books again for 'learning', umbrellas and can for 'transfer'), without AI; trained raters scored fluency, originality, and flexibility. fNIRS brain activity and self-reported bonding and interaction quality were also measured.

studies.label: Lab experiment: AI vs human vs no creativity instruction, AUT pre/post with fNIRS

assignment.what_was_assigned: Instruction type: AI instruction (ChatGPT-4.0 tutor), human instruction (trained human instructor), or control (quiet rest)
assignment.quote: They were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: AI (n = 31, 27 females), human (n = 34, 21 females), and control (n = 30, 28 females).
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 2.1 Participants; design described as 3 x 2 mixed (between: instruction type; within: pre vs post), p. 4, Section 2.3

arms.name: AI instruction
arms.description: One-to-one text chat with ChatGPT-4.0 acting as creativity instructor for about 8-10 min, after a brief standard guideline on how to set up a learning dialogue; backup learning materials on association, decomposition, adaptation, and combination were provided; chats were monitored by researchers.

arms.name: Human instruction
arms.description: Face-to-face, one-to-one heuristic dialogue with a postgraduate education student trained in lecturing, following a standardized script (association, decomposition, combination) for the same duration.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Sat quietly with eyes closed for the same duration, with no instruction or interaction.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions are reported. The analyzed count is read from the degrees of freedom: behavioral ANOVAs use F(2,92), consistent with all 95 participants (p. 5); AI vs human t-tests use t(63), consistent with 31 + 34 = 65 (p. 6).
participants.who: Right-handed adults recruited through university advertisements, mean age 21.82 (SD 2.44), 76 female, one to two years of comparable AI-tool experience, comparable educational backgrounds. The paper does not state that all were students.
participants.quote: To ensure sufficient sample size, 95 participants were recruited (76 females, Mean age = 21.82, SD = 2.44).

ai_tool.how_used: Participants chatted freely with ChatGPT in real time, cast as their creativity instructor; the guideline suggested prompts such as asking it to teach strategies for divergent thinking, asking how to generate more novel uses for books, and asking for more original ideas. AI was used only in the instruction phase, not during the scored post-test.

task.description: Alternative Uses Task: list as many creative uses as possible for an everyday object within 3 min per item. Pre-test item: books. Post-test items: books (learning/acquisition outcome) and umbrellas and can (transfer outcomes), order counterbalanced.
task.duration: Pre-test 3 min; instruction about 8-10 min; post-test 10 min (Fig. 1B, p. 4)

outcomes.name: Originality, learning item (books), post-test
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each de-duplicated idea rated 1-5 for originality by two trained independent raters (ICC 0.903-0.962), ratings averaged per participant. Printed AI post-test mean (34.91) exceeds 5, so the participant score appears to aggregate across ideas; the aggregation is not stated. Change scores (post minus pre) are also used in correlations (Fig. 6).
outcomes.delay: Post-test followed instruction after a 60 s rest

contrasts.reported: Time x instruction type interaction F(2,92) = 6.12, p = 0.003, partial eta^2 = 0.12 (three groups). AI post-test originality 34.91 +/- 10.80; AI post-test higher than human and control post-test, ps <= 0.04. Fig. 2B annotates AI vs control post-test p < 0.001. Control means and SDs only in Table S2 (supplement) and Fig. 2B.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to ChatGPT-4.0 creativity instruction, human instruction, or no instruction (p. 3); 95 people across arms, all apparently analyzed (F(2,92), p. 5); AUT fluency, originality, and flexibility were scored by trained raters on the post-test produced without AI, so all outcomes answer after_ai with immediate timing.

one_line_finding: After 8-10 min of ChatGPT-4.0 creativity instruction, unassisted AUT originality and flexibility on the practiced item and flexibility on novel items were higher than after human instruction or rest (e.g., learning originality interaction F(2,92) = 6.12, p = 0.003; transfer flexibility F(2,92) = 7.182, p = 0.001; p. 5-6, Fig. 2), with no clear fluency difference.
open_questions: Only the AI group's post-test means and SDs are printed; control and human-instruction means and SDs are in supplementary Table S2, which is not in this PDF.
The printed AI post-test flexibility on the learning item (7.29 +/- 2.97, p. 5) looks inconsistent with Fig. 2C, where the AI post-test bar is near 10 and the pre-test near 7; check Table S2.

The learning item (books) is the same object used in the AI guideline's example prompt ('different uses for books', p. 4), so AI-arm participants may have received AI-generated uses for the item they were then scored on; this matters for interpreting the learning outcome as unassisted.
How originality scores are aggregated per participant (sum vs mean of 1-5 ratings) and how the two transfer items are combined is not stated.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on the output: fNIRS brain activation (Delta HbO) and functional connectivity, self-reported affiliative bonding, interaction quality, perceived usefulness and ease of use, and learning motivation. Pre-test group equivalence: one-way ANOVAs, all ps >= 0.626 (p. 5). Post hoc between-group p-values for post-test scores appear in the text as ranges and in Fig. 2 annotations; no regression coefficients or standard errors are printed. The post-test order of the three AUT items was counterbalanced (p. 5). The trained raters' blinding to condition is not stated.
